clinicalPearls: The most frequent symptom prompting the diagnosis of a PID is recurrent or unusually severe infection; recurrent allergic or autoimmune manifestations may also be the alerting feature (Harrison 22e p.2793).

PIDs are classified by (1) the arm of the immune system that is defective and (2) the mechanism of the defect; the major categories are antibody/B-cell defects (agammaglobulinaemia, CVID, hyper-IgM, IgA deficiency), T-cell/cellular defects, combined defects (SCID), and innate-immune defects of phagocytes, complement, or innate receptors/signalling (Harrison 22e p.2794).

The site of infection and the causal microorganism point to the affected compartment: respiratory-tract (sinus, bronchial) infection mostly suggests defective antibody responses; invasive bacterial infection can result from complement deficiency, innate-signalling defects, asplenia, or antibody defects; viral, recurrent Candida, and opportunistic infections suggest impaired T-cell immunity; skin infections and deep abscesses primarily reflect innate (phagocyte) defects such as chronic granulomatous disease (Harrison 22e p.2794).

B-lymphocyte (antibody) deficiencies are the most frequent PIDs, accounting for 60-70% of all cases; T-cell deficiencies account for ~20% and innate-immune defects for ~10% (Harrison 22e p.2794, 2796, 2797).

Encapsulated/pyogenic bacteria (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis) and recurrent sinopulmonary infection are the hallmark of defective antibody production; untreated recurrent bronchial infection leads to bronchiectasis, cor pulmonale, and death (Harrison 22e p.2801).

Invasive Neisseria infection points to deficiencies of the complement lytic phase (C5-C9) or the alternative pathway (factors D, properdin); classic-pathway and lytic-phase complement deficiencies may also predispose to autoimmune disease, notably SLE (Harrison 22e p.2797).

CVID is recognised predominantly in adults, although clinical manifestations can begin earlier in life; in most cases no molecular cause is identified and the diagnosis is made only after excluding hypomorphic agammaglobulinaemia mutations and more subtle T-cell defects, especially in children (Harrison 22e p.2802).

First-line laboratory work-up is guided by the clinical picture and includes blood cell counts/morphology, serum immunoglobulin levels (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE), specific antibody responses to vaccines (tetanus toxoid, unconjugated pneumococcal polysaccharide), and lymphocyte subset phenotyping; more specific (genetic) tests then confirm a definitive diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2794-2795).

Even with profound B-cell deficiency, infections rarely occur before 6 months of age because of transplacental maternal IgG; conversely, in SCID clinical consequences typically appear within 3-6 months of birth (Harrison 22e p.2801, 2799).
Immunoglobulin replacement should be guided by the occurrence of infection, not by laboratory IgG/antibody levels alone, to avoid unjustified infusions; it is lifelong therapy (Harrison 22e p.2802).

A precise molecular/genetic diagnosis has become a milestone in the care of PID patients, guiding treatment selection, genetic counselling, and prenatal diagnosis; suspected cases should be referred to experienced centres (Harrison 22e p.2804).
harrison.pathophysiology: PIDs are predominantly Mendelian genetic diseases that arise whenever the expression or function of a nonredundant effector or mediator of the immune system is genetically impaired. More than 550 conditions have been described, with deleterious mutations identified in roughly 500 genes; estimated prevalence is 5-10 per 100,000 (probably an underestimate). They are increasingly grouped within the broader category of inborn errors of immunity that also includes autoinflammatory syndromes. Defects can involve any aspect of innate or adaptive immunity, cell differentiation, effector function, or immune regulation. The clinical consequence is multiple levels of vulnerability to infection, ranging from extremely broad (as in SCID, where T-cell development is blocked) to narrowly restricted to a single class of organism (as in Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease, an IL-12-IFN-gamma axis defect). Antibody (B-cell) defects (agammaglobulinaemia from BTK and pre-B-cell-receptor gene defects, hyper-IgM from class-switch-recombination defects such as CD40L/CD40, IgA deficiency, and CVID) impair production or class switching of immunoglobulins, leaving patients unable to opsonise and neutralise pyogenic encapsulated bacteria. Cellular (T-cell) defects impair help for antibody production, macrophage activation, and cytotoxicity, causing susceptibility to viral, fungal (Candida), and opportunistic infections (e.g., Pneumocystis jirovecii, Cryptosporidium). Combined defects (SCID) abolish both arms. Innate defects affect phagocyte number (severe congenital neutropenia), adhesion (LAD), or microbial killing (chronic granulomatous disease, from defective NADPH-oxidase reactive-oxygen-species production), as well as complement components and innate receptor/signalling pathways (TLR adaptors IRAK4/MYD88). Beyond infection, PIDs can drive immunopathology including allergy, lymphoproliferation, autoimmunity, and an increased risk of malignancy (notably lymphoma) (Harrison 22e p.2793-2794, 2796-2802).

harrison.prognosis: Prognosis varies widely with the molecule and arm of immunity affected. T-cell and combined defects generally carry a poor prognosis and require early diagnosis and intervention; SCID is fatal in infancy without treatment, but allogeneic HSCT offers a high curative potential in patients in otherwise reasonable condition, and gene therapy has succeeded in X-linked (gamma-c) SCID, ADA-SCID, and Artemis deficiency. Functional T-cell defects carry a worse HSCT prognosis than SCID because many patients are already chronically infected at diagnosis. For antibody deficiencies, lifelong immunoglobulin replacement combined with management of chronic lung disease reduces respiratory infections and prevents progression to bronchiectasis and cor pulmonale; in CVID, lymphoproliferation, granulomatous disease, autoimmunity, and lymphoma define long-term prognosis. DNA-repair disorders such as ataxia-telangiectasia are progressive and carry a very high risk of lymphoma, leukaemia, and (in adulthood) carcinoma. Newborn TREC screening, by enabling treatment of uninfected SCID patients, maximises the chance of cure. Early diagnosis with referral to experienced centres is essential to optimal outcome (Harrison 22e p.2794, 2799-2800, 2802, 2804).
pitfalls: CVID can present in adulthood and is easily missed; it is recognised predominantly in adults although manifestations may begin earlier (Harrison 22e p.2802).

High variability of expression for a given PID (e.g., WAS, XLA, CTLA4 deficiency) can hamper diagnosis; modifier genes and environmental triggers such as EBV (in XLP) modulate the phenotype (Harrison 22e p.2804).
Leaky BTK mutations causing mild hypogammaglobulinaemia with low but detectable B cells should not be confused with CVID (Harrison 22e p.2802).
T-cell lymphopenia in SCID may be masked by maternally-engrafted T cells, so screening for maternal cells with genetic markers should be performed when needed (Harrison 22e p.2799).

Somatic mutations in an affected gene can attenuate the phenotype of T-cell PIDs (described for ADA, X-linked SCID, RAG, NEMO, and most often WAS), while somatic mutations can also create PID-like disease (as in ALPS) (Harrison 22e p.2804).
Cytokine-neutralising autoantibodies (to IFN-gamma, IL-6, IL-7, type I interferon) can mimic a PID (Harrison 22e p.2804).

Caution with immunoglobulin replacement in patients with complete IgA deficiency and residual antibody production: anti-IgA antibodies can trigger anaphylactic shock, so IgA-free IgG preparations should be used (Harrison 22e p.2803).

Ataxia-telangiectasia should be considered in young children with IgA deficiency and recurrent problematic infections, as ataxia and telangiectasia may not appear before age 3-4 years (Harrison 22e p.2799-2800).
harrison.severityClassification: PIDs are classified along two axes: (1) the arm of the immune system that is defective and (2) the mechanism of the defect (when known). The two main divisions are deficiencies of the innate immune system (phagocytic cells - impaired production [severe congenital neutropenia], asplenia, impaired adhesion [LAD], impaired killing [CGD]; innate-immunity receptors/signal transduction [TLR-signalling defects, MSMD]; complement deficiencies of the classical/alternative/lectin pathways and the lytic phase) and deficiencies of the adaptive immune system (T lymphocytes - SCID, DiGeorge, combined immunodeficiencies, hyper-IgE, DOCK8, CD40L, Wiskott-Aldrich, ataxia-telangiectasia and DNA-repair defects; B lymphocytes - X-linked/AR agammaglobulinaemia, hyper-IgM, CVID, IgA deficiency), together with regulatory defects (autoinflammatory syndromes, severe colitis, HLH, ALPS, autoimmunity such as IPEX and APECED). The classification is acknowledged to involve some arbitrary decisions because of overlap and incomplete data (Harrison 22e p.2794).
management: Immunoglobulin replacement therapy, given intravenously or subcutaneously, as the mainstay for antibody and B-cell deficiencies
Prompt aggressive treatment of infection plus targeted prophylaxis, such as co-trimoxazole against Pneumocystis in T-cell defects and antifungal or antiviral prophylaxis as dictated by the defect
Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for severe combined and other profound cellular defects, with gene therapy for selected disorders such as adenosine deaminase deficiency
Avoidance of live vaccines in severe T-cell or combined defects, use of irradiated cytomegalovirus-safe blood products, and appropriate immunisation of antibody-deficient patients and their contacts
Management of end-organ complications, including airway clearance and treatment of bronchiectasis, and immunomodulation for autoimmune or inflammatory manifestations
Regular surveillance of organ function, growth and infection burden, with immune reconstitution monitoring after transplantation
Care coordinated by a specialist clinical immunology centre within a multidisciplinary team
Genetic counselling and family screening, with access to newborn screening that enables early detection of severe combined immunodeficiency
